gaps.sentence: We see our grandparents ___ other weekend.
gaps.explanation: 'Every other weekend' means alternate weekends; 'each other' has a different, reciprocal meaning.

gaps.sentence: I asked ___ in the office, but nobody knew the answer.
gaps.explanation: 'I asked everybody' (all the people) contrasts with 'nobody knew'; 'everything' refers to things, not people.

gaps.sentence: There was ___ enthusiasm for the proposal, so it was quietly shelved.
gaps.explanation: 'Little' (without 'a') means not enough — which explains shelving the proposal.

gaps.sentence: ___ students joined the trip this year than last.
___ of the students has been given a personal timetable.
gaps.hint: this is the only option that can be followed by 'of' and take a singular verb
gaps.explanation: 'Each of the students has ...' is correct; 'every' cannot take 'of' here and 'all/both' need a plural verb.

gaps.sentence: There were ___ people in the lift, and it broke down.
gaps.explanation: 'Too many' is used before countable plurals like people; 'too much' is for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: He made a ___ of money in property.
gaps.hint: the article 'a' is already in the sentence
gaps.explanation: 'A lot of money' is the fixed phrase; 'a lots of', 'a plenty of' and 'a deal of' do not exist.

gaps.sentence: ___ money was spent on advertising last year.
